clue.text: Why athlete may go to ground expecting punishment?

definitions.text: Why athlete may go to ground
definitions.meaning: a jumper heads to the sports ground to compete in one particular field event
a British idiom for someone who is in serious trouble and about to be disciplined

explanation.surface: A sportsman trudging off to the stadium as if heading for a telling-off.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first half literally: the athlete goes to the ground to compete in the high jump. 'Ground' is a sports ground, not the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a person facing a severe reprimand or penalty is said to be in for this, so the idiom matches awaiting chastisement.

clue.text: Traditionally, Adam and Eve people not previously in suits

definitions.meaning: in the Genesis story this couple committed the original sin before anyone else
suits here are lawsuits: these people have never before been prosecuted

explanation.surface: Adam and Eve pictured as naked, never having worn a suit of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suits' pretends to be clothing, which fits a naked Adam and Eve; it actually means legal cases, so the second half describes someone with no criminal record.
explanation.definitionFit: Courts use this term for defendants convicted for the first time, and the biblical pair were the earliest sinners in tradition.

clue.text: Another impression touching children

parts.note: re = touching, in the sense of concerning or about
issue = offspring, a legal word for children

explanation.surface: A second impression made by something touching the children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impression' is a printing of a book, not a feeling or an imitation; a second printing is a fresh release of the same work.
explanation.definitionFit: In publishing an impression is a print run, so a further print run of a book is the same thing as a new release.

clue.text: Bats breathe in and sleep for months

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the letters that follow are in a mad jumble

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Bats taking a deep breath and settling in for the long winter sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the animals, which really do spend winter dormant; here it is the adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals such as bears and bats pass the winter in a dormant state, which is exactly a very long seasonal slumber.

clue.text: Cow loose in house — what's the explanation?

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another sits within it

parts.note: a house is a home

indicators.note: something set loose is free to wander out of its usual order

parts.note: fodder for the anagram, three letters

explanation.surface: A cow wandering loose indoors, and someone demanding to know why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose' and 'in' both look like part of the farmyard picture; each is an instruction, and 'house' must be swapped for a synonym before anything goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal phrase is a colloquial way of asking why, i.e. requesting the reason for something surprising.

clue.text: Most gloomy feature of ogre? Yes, thankfully

indicators.note: a feature is a part of a thing, so the letters are a part of the words that follow

parts.note: letters run across the three words, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: Someone relieved that an ogre's grimmest feature turns out to be only that.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and comma break up the surface but the letters run straight through: o-GRE YES-T hankfully.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey weather or grey moods are dull and cheerless, so the superlative of that colour means the dreariest or dullest.

clue.text: Well I never! Our queen's scrapped service vehicles

indicators.note: what has been scrapped is thrown away, so it leaves the word

parts.note: an exclamation of surprise
ER = Elizabeth Regina, the removed piece

explanation.surface: Someone astonished that the monarch has got rid of her army vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ER out of the middle of JEEPERS. 'Service' means the armed services, not a church service or a garage service.
explanation.definitionFit: These rugged four-wheel-drive cars were developed for the US army and are classic military transport.

clue.text: Mother's wise treatment for stress

parts.note: Ma's = mother's
sage = wise

explanation.surface: A mother's sensible remedy for a frazzled child.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests homespun advice; the apostrophe S is a letter in the answer, not just possession.
explanation.definitionFit: Kneading the muscles is a common therapy used to relieve tension and help a person relax.

clue.text: Quotes from "Hamlet", say

parts.note: surface reading: famous lines taken from Shakespeare's play
setter's reading: the punctuation marks printed around the title in the clue itself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quotes' reads as quotations from the play, but it means quotation marks, and the clue shows a pair of them wrapped around the title.
explanation.definitionFit: British English calls quotation marks by this name, and quotes is a common short form for those same punctuation marks.

clue.text: A colourful display from the Gunners in East End

parts.note: RA = Royal Artillery, whose soldiers are gunners
used as it stands
Bow is a district in London's East End

explanation.surface: Fireworks laid on by Arsenal fans (the Gunners) somewhere in east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Gunners' suggests Arsenal football club, but it is the Royal Artillery; 'in' is not a container signal here, just two letters in the chain.
explanation.definitionFit: An arc of spectral colours seen in the sky after rain is a natural spectacle made of many hues.

clue.text: US author's someone not initially gripping me

indicators.note: not at the start means the opening letter is dropped
to grip is to hold, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a person, minus the P at the front
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A literary puzzle about some unnamed person wrapping their arms around the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Someone' has to be turned into a word before its first letter can go. Ralph Waldo Emerson was the American essayist and poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson was a nineteenth-century American essayist and transcendentalist writer, so he is an author from the States.

clue.text: Police weapon that a sergeant uses

indicators.note: the words make use of these letters, carrying them inside themselves

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A sergeant's choice of equipment on the beat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is complete and plausible, which hides the fact that the answer is lying in plain sight across tha-T A SER-geant.
explanation.definitionFit: This electroshock stun gun is carried by many officers to subdue suspects without firing bullets.

clue.text: Where president has the authority to exaggerate

definitions.meaning: a president holds power above the nation, read as two words
the ordinary verb sense, to make something seem bigger than it is

explanation.surface: A president given the power to inflate the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as OVER STATE: a president is in charge of, or over, the state.
explanation.definitionFit: To claim more than is true or make something sound larger is simply to overdo a description, the plain verb meaning.

clue.text: Loud rampaging teenager, one without restraint

parts.note: f = forte, loud in music

indicators.note: rampaging means running wild, so the letters run out of control

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A noisy teenager running riot, answerable to nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: F comes first, then the rearranged TEENAGER. The surface picture of an unruly youth fits the definition nicely.
explanation.definitionFit: A person not bound to any employer, team or master can act independently and is not tied down by obligations.

clue.text: Council leader handed down rent

indicators.note: the leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of council
left = bequeathed, as in a will

explanation.surface: A council boss passing down a decision on housing rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is not money for housing but the past participle of rend, torn apart; 'handed down' means bequeathed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something split or torn apart: rent is the old past participle of rend, and the answer is split open.

clue.text: It could make DG conceal rustic entertainment

indicators.note: the letters could be made into something new, so they are rebuilt in a fresh order

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A Director-General hiding some country amusement from view.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals DG look like an abbreviation to be expanded, but they are just two letters of fodder for the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A folk step performed in wooden shoes is a traditional country pastime danced at village fairs.

clue.text: Follow those last in line then, unless you leave

indicators.note: only the final letter of each of the following words is kept

parts.note: the final letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: An order to join the back of a queue unless you are going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last in line' looks like a queue, but 'those last in' takes the ends of line, then, unless, you, leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To come after as a result or in sequence is the meaning of the verb, as in trouble that comes afterwards.

clue.text: Large bird seen above the main city of Wales

indicators.note: in a down entry the upper piece is written first

parts.note: a swan is a large waterbird
the main = the open sea, an old poetic term

explanation.surface: A swan flying above the chief city of Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' pretends to be an adjective, principal, but it is the noun meaning the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: This coastal place in south Wales is the country's second-largest urban centre after Cardiff.

clue.text: Fellow stalwart in action, sacked from the ministry

indicators.note: one thing placed inside another sits within it

parts.note: a deed is an act
F = fellow, a standard abbreviation
a rock is someone utterly dependable

explanation.surface: A loyal colleague dismissed from a government department after some incident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ministry' reads as a government department, but it is the church ministry, whose priests wear a frock; 'fellow' is the standard abbreviation F.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest formally stripped of clerical status loses the right to wear the frock, so he is expelled from holy orders.

clue.text: Daughter replacing leader in gym exercise put costume on

indicators.note: one letter takes the place of the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: D = daughter, a standard abbreviation
a press-up, minus its opening P

explanation.surface: A daughter swapping her gym workout for a costume party.
explanation.walkthrough: A press-up is the British name for a push-up; D takes the place of its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Children who put on fancy clothes to play pretend are wearing disguises, which is the phrasal verb's meaning.

clue.text: Skilful handling's needed when imposing penalties on bridge players

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece sitting on another comes before it

parts.note: fines are monetary penalties
South and East are two of the four seats at a bridge table

explanation.surface: Tact is required when penalising a bridge team.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge players sit as North, South, East and West, so any pair of compass letters can stand for them; the answer is also a bridge term, a neat touch.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names delicacy and subtle skill in dealing with a situation, and is also a card-playing manoeuvre.

clue.text: Relations summon up a particular form of energy

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase; the answer is the adjective naming that energy

parts.note: kin = relatives

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: to cite is to summon to court

explanation.surface: Calling the relatives together to generate some special kind of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summon up' looks like a phrasal verb meaning muster, but 'up' is the reversal signal and 'summon' alone is the legal cite.
explanation.definitionFit: Physics distinguishes motion energy from potential energy, and this adjective names the type possessed by a moving body.

clue.text: Dame Edna's one to pull man on board

parts.note: to drag is to pull
a chess piece, a man on the chessboard

explanation.surface: Dame Edna trying to seduce a man aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' suggests a sailor, but it is a chessman. Dame Edna Everage was the stage character of the male comedian Barry Humphries.
explanation.definitionFit: Barry Humphries performed in women's clothing as the character, making Dame Edna a famous example of a female-impersonating entertainer.

clue.text: Where ships may draw up report of security devices

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the sound of the word is what counts

parts.note: keys secure locks; the two words are pronounced identically in British English

explanation.surface: Ships drawing up a report about their security equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw up' pretends to mean write up a document, which leads nicely into 'report'; really it means come alongside and stop.
explanation.definitionFit: These are stone or concrete landing platforms beside water where vessels moor to load and unload.

clue.text: Couple penning notes haven't a clue

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a duo is a pair
N = note, twice

explanation.surface: A couple writing notes to each other, stumped by a crossword clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penning' looks like writing, but it means enclosing, as sheep in a pen.
explanation.definitionFit: This slangy contraction of I do not know is what someone says when completely ignorant of the matter.

clue.text: Artist's cries disheartened villains

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the central letter

parts.note: RA = Royal Academician, a crossword artist, with the 's
calls, with one of its middle L's removed

explanation.surface: An artist's anguished cries as he gives up hope over some villains.
explanation.walkthrough: CALLS has five letters, so its heart is the middle letter, the second L.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes rogues and scoundrels, dishonest people, though today it is often used playfully of mischievous children.

clue.text: Retreat, it's said, diminished corporation

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so we want the sound rather than the spelling

parts.note: sank = fell away or dwindled
corporation is jokey British slang for a large belly, a tum

explanation.surface: A company closing its offices after shrinking in size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' pretends to be a business; in old British slang it means a paunch, a pot belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A private room or sacred inner place where someone can hide away undisturbed is a refuge from the world.

clue.text: Confused prelates taken in by criminals' deceptions

indicators.note: whatever is taken in by something ends up inside it

parts.note: fences are criminals who deal in stolen goods

indicators.note: confused letters have lost their proper order

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Bewildered bishops conned by crooks' tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: Prelates are bishops, but here the word is only raw letters. A fence is a receiver of stolen goods, a common crossword criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal phrase names obtaining something by lying about facts, so it covers trickery and fraud in general.
